skills.title: Infer a character's feelings and motives from actions and clues in a story
State the message of a story in one or two sentences of their own (asking questions opens the way to learning)
Form wh-questions correctly with a helper verb or do/does before the subject
Work out word meanings from context and build word families (curious - curiosity, eager - eagerly)

expectations: Says that the girl wants to learn but has been kept at home while others go to school
Infers her feeling (left out, sad, longing) from a clue in the story, not just from a stated word
Says the message: asking questions and speaking up is how learning starts; every child has a right to learn
Links one event to the message (her question to the river leads her to the headmaster)
Asks at least one correct wh-question of their own about the story

misconceptions.belief: A question is made by putting a question word in front of a statement, as in Hindi ('Tum kyun udaas ho?' becomes 'Why you are sad?')
signs: Says 'Why you are sad?'
Says 'Where the river goes?'
Says 'What you want to learn?'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which question is correct: 'Why you are sad, Meenu?' or 'Why are you sad, Meenu?'
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Dono suno — 'Why you are sad?' aur 'Why are you sad?'. English mein sawaal kaunsa sahi banta hai?

options.text: Why are you sad, Meenu?
Why you are sad, Meenu?

remediation.representation: Word cards: the subject card and the helper card swap places to turn a statement into a question ('you ARE' becomes 'ARE you'); when there is no helper, a do/does card slides in
remediation.moveShape: Child says the statement, physically swaps helper and subject cards, then says the question aloud; teacher brings in the do/does card for verbs with no helper

misconceptions.belief: After 'does', the main verb still keeps its -s or -es
signs: Says 'Where does the river flows?'
Says 'Does she wants to study?'
Says 'Why does he goes?'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'Where does the river go?' or 'Where does the river goes?'
diagnostic.prompt_hi: 'does' ke baad verb kaisa hoga? 'Where does the river go?' ya 'Where does the river goes?'

options.text: Where does the river go?
Where does the river goes?

remediation.representation: A single -s token that can sit on 'does' or on the verb, but never on both at once
remediation.moveShape: Child moves the -s token from 'flows' onto 'do' to make 'does', and notices the verb goes back to its base form; repeat with two more verbs

misconceptions.belief: A character feels only what the story says in a feeling word; if no feeling word is written, we cannot know
signs: Answers 'The story doesn't say' when asked how a character feels
Describes the action ('she was sitting') instead of the feeling
Cannot point to a clue for a feeling

diagnostic.prompt_en: Meenu watched her brothers walk to school and threw a stone into the river. How did she most likely feel?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Meenu ne bhaiyon ko school jaate dekha aur paani mein patthar phenka. Usne kaisa feel kiya hoga?

options.text: Left out and sad that she could not go
We cannot know, the story does not say
Happy, because she likes stones

remediation.representation: A clue-to-feeling chart with three columns: what the character does, what that shows, the feeling word
remediation.moveShape: Teacher thinks aloud through one clue, child fills the next row; then child names the feeling and the clue that proves it

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every evening, Meenu sat by the river while her brothers did homework. "Why can't I go to school too?" she asked. The river seemed to whisper, "Keep asking. Every question is a small step." Next morning, Meenu walked to the headmaster's door.' Where did Meenu sit every evening?
items.prompt_hi: Kahani suno. Meenu har shaam kahaan baithti thi?
items.answer: By the river
hints: Listen to the first line again.
It is a place with water.
Every evening, Meenu sat by the ___.
She sat by the river.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every evening, Meenu sat by the river while her brothers did homework. "Why can't I go to school too?" she asked. The river seemed to whisper, "Keep asking. Every question is a small step." Next morning, Meenu walked to the headmaster's door.' Why do you think Meenu asked the river her question, and not her family?
items.prompt_hi: Socho — Meenu ne apna sawaal ghar walon se kyun nahi, nadi se poocha?
items.answer: She felt no one at home would listen or say yes, so she shared her feelings with the river, which felt like a safe friend
acceptable: she was afraid to ask her family
the river was like a friend
she was shy to ask at home
hints: What is she doing while her brothers study?
Think about how she feels at home.
Maybe she was afraid her family would ___.
She felt unheard at home, so she spoke to the river like a friend.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Every evening, Meenu sat by the river while her brothers did homework. "Why can't I go to school too?" she asked. The river seemed to whisper, "Keep asking. Every question is a small step." Next morning, Meenu walked to the headmaster's door.' What do you think Meenu will say to the headmaster?
items.prompt_hi: Agla kya hoga? Headmaster ke darwaaze par Meenu kya bolegi?
items.answer: She will ask if she can join the school and learn to read
acceptable: she will ask to join school
she will ask to learn to read
hints: What does she want most in the story?
Think of what she asked the river.
She will ask whether she can ___ school.
She will ask to join the school and learn to read.

items.prompt_en: Make a question beginning with 'Why' from this sentence: 'The river flows to the sea.'
items.prompt_hi: Is sentence se 'Why' wala sawaal banao: 'The river flows to the sea.' Dhyaan do — 'does' chahiye.
items.answer: Why does the river flow to the sea?
acceptable: Why does the river flow to the sea?
Why does it flow to the sea?
hints: Is there a helper verb like is or can?
No helper, so bring in do or does.
Why ___ the river ___ to the sea?
Why does the river flow to the sea? The -s moves to does.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake and say it correctly: 'Why you are sad, Meenu?'
items.prompt_hi: Is sawaal mein galti dhoondho: 'Why you are sad, Meenu?'
items.answer: Why are you sad, Meenu?
hints: Look at the words after 'Why'.
In a question, the helper verb comes before the subject.
Why ___ you sad?
It should be 'Why are you sad, Meenu?'

items.prompt_en: Listen to two sentences: 'Where does the river go?' and 'Where the river goes is a mystery.' Which one is a question, and how do you know?
items.prompt_hi: Do sentences hain. Kaunsa sawaal hai, aur kaise pata chala?
items.answer: 'Where does the river go?' is the question, because 'does' comes before the subject 'the river'
acceptable: the first, because does comes before the river
hints: Which one ends with a question mark?
Look for a helper word before the subject.
In the question, '___' comes before 'the river'.
The first is the question: 'does' comes before the subject.

items.prompt_en: Ask a question about time from this sentence, starting with 'When': 'The school bell rings at nine.'
items.prompt_hi: Ab 'When' se sawaal banao: 'The school bell rings at nine.'
items.answer: When does the school bell ring?
acceptable: When does the school bell ring?
hints: What helper word do we need here?
One bell, so use 'does'.
When ___ the school bell ___?
When does the school bell ring? The -s goes onto does.

items.prompt_en: 'The river seemed to whisper, Keep asking.' What does 'whisper' mean here: shout loudly, speak very softly, or run fast?
items.prompt_hi: 'Whisper' ka matlab kya hai yahaan? Zor se chillana, bahut dheere bolna, ya tez bhaagna?
items.answer: Speak very softly
hints: Imagine the sound of slow water.
Is it loud or quiet?
To whisper is to speak very ___.
Whisper means to speak very softly.

items.prompt_en: Say this in English using the word 'eager': 'Meenu ko padhne ki bahut ichchha thi.'
items.prompt_hi: Is Hindi line ko English mein bolo, 'eager' word use karke: 'Meenu ko padhne ki bahut ichchha thi.'
items.answer: Meenu was eager to study.
acceptable: Meenu was very eager to study.
Meenu was very eager to learn.
hints: Who is the sentence about?
Use 'was eager to' plus an action.
Meenu was eager to ___.
Meenu was eager to study.

items.prompt_en: 'Curious' is an adjective. Fill the blank with its noun: 'Her ___ made her ask many questions.'
items.prompt_hi: 'Curious' ka naam-shabd (noun) kya hoga? 'Her ___ made her ask many questions.'
items.answer: curiosity
hints: The blank needs a naming word, not a describing word.
Change the ending of 'curious'.
curious becomes curi-o-___
The noun is curiosity.

items.prompt_en: In the story, the river says, 'Every question is a small step.' What does the writer want us to understand from this?
items.prompt_hi: Nadi kehti hai 'Every question is a small step.' Lekhak hume kya samjhana chahte hain?
items.answer: Asking questions is how learning begins, so we should not be afraid to ask
acceptable: do not be afraid to ask
hints: A step towards what?
What did Meenu's question lead her to do?
Each question takes us closer to ___.
Questions are how learning begins, so keep asking.

items.prompt_en: Your little cousin asks, 'Why is the story of the girl and the river important?' Explain its big message to her in two or three sentences.
items.prompt_hi: Chhoti cousin ko samjhao — nadi aur ladki wali kahani ka asli sandesh kya hai? Do-teen line mein.
items.answer: The girl wants to learn but is kept at home; by asking questions and speaking up she finds her way to school, so every child, girls too, deserves to learn and should keep asking
acceptable: every child should get to learn
girls also have the right to study
asking questions opens the door to learning
speak up for what you want to learn
hints: What did the girl want?
What did she do about it?
Her questions led her to ___.
Every child deserves to learn, and asking questions opens the way.

workedExample.problem: Make a 'Why' question from: 'Meenu stays at home.'
steps: Find the subject and verb: subject 'Meenu', verb 'stays'.
There is no helper verb, so bring in 'does' (Meenu is one person).
Put 'Why' first, then 'does', then the subject 'Meenu'.
Move the -s from 'stays' onto 'does', so the verb becomes 'stay'.
Answer: Why does Meenu stay at home?
fadedVersion: Find the subject and verb: subject '___', verb 'stays'.
There is no helper verb, so bring in '___'.
Put 'Why' first, then 'does', then the ___.
Move the -s from 'stays' onto 'does', so the verb becomes '___'.
Answer: Why ___ Meenu ___ at home?

skills.title: Read a short poem aloud with rhythm, stressing the repeated line (refrain)
Explain the central idea of a poem about perseverance and how repetition carries it
Identify rhyming pairs and the rhyme scheme of a stanza (AABB, ABAB)
Use the first conditional correctly: If + present, will + base verb

expectations: States the central idea: when you fail, do not give up; try again and keep practising
Explains why the refrain is repeated (it drills the message into the reader, like practice itself)
Names at least one rhyming pair and the stanza's rhyme scheme
Gives an example from real life of trying again after failing
Uses a correct first-conditional sentence ('If you practise, you will improve')

misconceptions.belief: Because the action is in the future, 'will' must go in the if-part too ('If you will try, you will win')
signs: Says 'If you will practise, you will win'
Says 'If it will rain, we will stay home'
Uses 'will' twice in one conditional

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'If you try again, you will succeed' or 'If you will try again, you will succeed'?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Kaunsa sahi hai? 'If you try again, you will succeed' ya 'If you will try again, you will succeed'?

options.text: If you try again, you will succeed.
If you will try again, you will succeed.

remediation.representation: A two-box sentence frame: the IF box holds only the present tense, the RESULT box holds 'will'; a 'will' card that does not fit in the IF box
remediation.moveShape: Child tries to place the 'will' card in the IF box and the teacher shows it bounces out; child builds three sentences with present in IF and will in RESULT

misconceptions.belief: Words rhyme only if they end in the same letters
signs: Says 'again' and 'rain' rhyme but 'again' and 'then' do not, judging by letters
Says 'won' and 'one' do not rhyme
Matches 'cough' with 'though'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Listen only to the sounds: do 'won' and 'one' rhyme?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Sirf awaaz suno, spelling mat dekho — 'won' aur 'one' rhyme karte hain kya?

options.text: Yes, they sound the same at the end
No, the letters are different

remediation.representation: Sound bars under each word: the ending sound lights up the same colour even when the letters differ
remediation.moveShape: Cover the spelling, say both words slowly, child judges by ear; then reveal the spelling as a surprise

misconceptions.belief: A poem about trying again is only about the one task it names (a kite, a climb), not a lesson for life
signs: Says the poem is 'about flying a kite'
Cannot apply the idea to studies or sport
Retells the lines instead of the idea

diagnostic.prompt_en: A poem tells of a boy whose kite falls again and again until it flies. What is the poem mainly about?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Ek kavita mein ladke ki patang baar-baar girti hai, phir udti hai. Kavita asal mein kis baare mein hai?

options.text: Not giving up when things go wrong
How to make a kite
Windy weather

remediation.representation: A bridge diagram: the poem's event (kite falls, rises) on one side, the life lesson on the other, with the child's own example in the middle
remediation.moveShape: Child names the event, then the teacher asks where else in life the same thing happens; child supplies their own example before stating the idea

items.prompt_en: Read these lines aloud and clap on the strong beats: 'The rope was high, my arms were sore, / I fell, I rose, I tried once more.' Which words get the strongest beat at the end of each line?
items.prompt_hi: Ye do lines taali ke saath padho. Har line ke aakhir mein kis word par sabse zor aata hai?
items.answer: sore and more
hints: Say the first line slowly.
Listen to where your voice lands at the end.
Line one ends on ___, line two ends on ___.
The strong beats land on 'sore' and 'more'.

items.prompt_en: In 'The rope was high, my arms were sore, / I fell, I rose, I tried once more,' which two words rhyme?
items.prompt_hi: In lines mein kaunse do words rhyme karte hain?
items.answer: sore and more
hints: Look at the last word of each line.
Say them one after the other.
S-ore and m-___
'Sore' and 'more' rhyme.

items.prompt_en: Listen only to the sounds. Which pair rhymes: 'won - one' or 'won - win'?
items.prompt_hi: Spelling bhool jao, sirf suno. Kaunsa joda rhyme karta hai: 'won-one' ya 'won-win'?
items.answer: won - one
hints: Say each pair aloud.
Rhyme is about the ending sound, not letters.
won and o-___ sound alike.
'Won' and 'one' rhyme; the spelling just looks different.

items.prompt_en: Here is a stanza: 'The seed lay deep beneath the ground, / It pushed and pushed without a sound, / The rain came down, the sun came out, / And up it came, a tiny sprout.' What is its rhyme scheme?
items.prompt_hi: Is stanza ki rhyme scheme kya hai? Har line ke aakhri word ko letter do — A, B…
items.answer: AABB
hints: Give the first line's end sound the letter A.
Does line two match line one?
ground/sound = A A, out/sprout = ___
The scheme is AABB.

items.prompt_en: Poems on trying again often repeat one line, like 'Try, try again'. Why does the poet repeat it so many times?
items.prompt_hi: Kavi ek hi line baar-baar kyun dohraate hain? Socho.
items.answer: Repetition fixes the message in our mind, and the repeating itself is like trying again and again
acceptable: it is like trying again and again
hints: What happens to a line you hear many times?
Think about what the poem is telling us to do.
Repeating helps us ___ the message.
Repetition drills the message in, just like practice.

items.prompt_en: A poem tells of a boy whose kite falls again and again until, at last, it flies high. What is the poem really about?
items.prompt_hi: Patang wali kavita asal mein kis baare mein hai? Sirf patang ke baare mein?
items.answer: Not giving up after failing; keep trying until you succeed
hints: Is it just about kites?
What does the boy keep doing?
The kite is a picture of ___.
It is about perseverance: keep trying after you fail.

items.prompt_en: Complete the sentence: 'If you ___ (practise) every day, you ___ (get) better at the guitar.'
items.prompt_hi: Khaali jagah bharo: 'If you ___ (practise) every day, you ___ (get) better.'
items.answer: If you practise every day, you will get better at the guitar.
acceptable: If you practise every day, you will get better
hints: Which part is the condition?
The if-part stays in the present.
If you ___ every day, you will ___ better.
If you practise every day, you will get better.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake: 'If you will try again, you will succeed.'
items.prompt_hi: Is sentence mein galti kahaan hai: 'If you will try again, you will succeed.'
items.answer: If you try again, you will succeed.
acceptable: If you try again, you will succeed.
hints: How many times is 'will' used?
Which part should be in the present tense?
If you ___ again, you will succeed.
Drop the first 'will': If you try again, you will succeed.

items.prompt_en: Say in English using 'if': 'Agar tum haar nahi maanoge, to tum jeetoge.'
items.prompt_hi: Isko English mein bolo, 'if' lagaakar: 'Agar tum haar nahi maanoge, to tum jeetoge.'
items.answer: If you do not give up, you will win.
acceptable: If you don't give up, you will win.
If you do not give up, you will win.
If you don't give up, you'll win.
If you never give up, you will win.
hints: Hindi says 'maanoge', but English if-part uses present.
'Haar maanna' is 'give up'.
If you don't ___, you will ___.
If you don't give up, you will win.

items.prompt_en: A girl misses the first three baskets at basketball practice. Her friend laughs. If she follows the idea of 'Try Again', what will she do next?
items.prompt_hi: Agar ladki 'Try Again' wali baat maane, to aage kya karegi?
items.answer: She will keep practising and try again until she scores
hints: What does the poem tell us to do after failing?
Does she stop or continue?
She will ___ again.
She will keep practising and try again.

items.prompt_en: What is a refrain in a poem?
items.prompt_hi: Kavita mein 'refrain' kya hota hai?
items.answer: A line or phrase that is repeated, often at the end of each stanza
acceptable: the line that comes again and again
hints: Think of a song's chorus.
It comes back again and again.
A refrain is a ___ line.
A refrain is a line repeated through the poem.

items.prompt_en: Your younger brother failed his cycling test and wants to quit. Explain the idea of the poem 'Try Again' to him, and give him one example.
items.prompt_hi: Chhote bhai ko 'Try Again' ka matlab samjhao, aur ek example bhi do.
items.answer: Failing once is normal; keep trying, because each try teaches you something and success comes with practice
acceptable: failure is a step to success
keep trying and you will improve
do not give up after one failure
hints: What happened to the boy in the kite poem?
What does each try teach you?
If at first you fail, ___ again.
Failing is normal; keep trying and practice brings success.

workedExample.problem: Complete: 'If Riya ___ (study) every day, she ___ (pass) the test.'
steps: Find the condition part: it starts with 'If'.
The if-part takes the simple present: Riya (she) studies.
The result part takes 'will' + base verb: will pass.
Answer: If Riya studies every day, she will pass the test.
fadedVersion: Find the condition part: it starts with '___'.
The if-part takes the simple ___: Riya studies.
The result part takes '___' + base verb.
Answer: If Riya ___ every day, she ___ the test.

skills.title: Find the main idea of a reflective passage and separate it from supporting details
Explain the writer's purpose: to make the reader value the senses they have
Use the second conditional for imagined situations: If + past, would + base verb
Choose precise sense verbs (see, look at, watch, gaze; hear, listen to) in context

expectations: States the main idea: people who can see often take sight for granted; we should use our senses fully
Names one detail that supports it (faces of loved ones, sunrise, stars)
Explains why the writer imagines only a few days of sight (to make us feel how precious each sight is)
Mentions that Helen Keller was blind and deaf, which gives her words force
Uses a correct second-conditional sentence about an imagined situation

misconceptions.belief: An imagined situation can mix present and would ('If I have three days, I would...')
signs: Says 'If I have wings, I would fly'
Says 'If I will see, I would...'
Mixes have/would in the same sentence

diagnostic.prompt_en: Helen Keller imagines having sight. Which is correct: 'If I had three days to see, I would look at my friends' faces' or 'If I have three days to see, I would look at my friends' faces'?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Yeh kalpana hai, sach nahi. To kaunsa sahi: 'If I had three days…, I would…' ya 'If I have three days…, I would…'?

options.text: If I had three days to see, I would look at my friends' faces.
If I have three days to see, I would look at my friends' faces.

remediation.representation: Two doors: a REAL door (If + present, will) and a DREAM door (If + past, would); each sentence card must go through one door with matching parts
remediation.moveShape: Child sorts sentence cards into real and imagined, then fixes mismatched ones by changing the verb in the if-part

misconceptions.belief: 'See', 'look' and 'watch' mean the same and can be swapped anywhere (Hindi 'dekhna' for all)
signs: Says 'I am seeing TV'
Says 'Look the stars'
Says 'Watch at the picture'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'I watched the cricket match on TV' or 'I saw at the cricket match on TV'?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hindi mein sab 'dekhna' hai, par English mein alag. Kaunsa sahi: 'I watched the cricket match' ya 'I saw at the cricket match'?

options.text: I watched the cricket match on TV.
I saw at the cricket match on TV.

remediation.representation: A three-step scale: see (happens to your eyes), look at (you turn your eyes on purpose), watch (you keep looking at something that moves or changes)
remediation.moveShape: Child acts each verb out (eyes open, turn head to a picture, follow a moving pen) and then picks the verb for three new sentences

misconceptions.belief: The main idea of a passage is its most vivid detail (the stars, the sunrise)
signs: Says the passage is 'about stars'
Lists details when asked for the main idea
Cannot say what all the details have in common

diagnostic.prompt_en: The writer talks about faces, a sunrise, and stars. What is the main idea?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Writer chehre, sunrise aur taaron ki baat karti hai. Inmein main idea kya hai?

options.text: We should value our sight and not take it for granted
Stars are beautiful at night
Gardens are nice in the morning

remediation.representation: An umbrella diagram: details hang below as raindrops, the main idea is the umbrella that covers all of them
remediation.moveShape: Child places each detail under the umbrella, then asks what single idea covers all three; teacher withholds the label until the child tries

items.prompt_en: Read: 'If I could see for just one day, I would first look at the faces of the people I love. I would walk in a garden at sunrise and watch the colours change. At night, I would gaze at the stars and try to hold them in my memory. Those of us who can see often forget how lucky we are.' What would the writer look at first?
items.prompt_hi: Passage suno. Writer sabse pehle kya dekhna chahti hai?
items.answer: The faces of the people she loves
acceptable: faces of the people she loves
the faces of people she loves
hints: Listen to the first sentence.
It is about people, not nature.
She would first look at the ___ of people she loves.
The faces of the people she loves.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'If I could see for just one day, I would first look at the faces of the people I love. I would walk in a garden at sunrise and watch the colours change. At night, I would gaze at the stars and try to hold them in my memory. Those of us who can see often forget how lucky we are.' Which sentence gives the main idea of the passage?
items.prompt_hi: Inmein se kaunsi line poore passage ka main idea batati hai?
items.answer: Those of us who can see often forget how lucky we are.
acceptable: those who can see forget how lucky they are
we forget how lucky we are to see
hints: Which sentence covers all the other details?
Look at the end of the passage.
Those of us who can see often forget how ___ we are.
The last sentence gives the main idea.

items.prompt_en: Which is the main idea and which is a detail? (a) 'At night, I would gaze at the stars.' (b) 'People who can see often take sight for granted.'
items.prompt_hi: Ek main idea hai, ek detail. Kaunsa kaunsa?
items.answer: (b) is the main idea and (a) is a detail
acceptable: b is main idea, a is detail
hints: Which one could cover many examples?
A detail is one example.
Gazing at stars is one ___.
(b) is the main idea; (a) is one detail that supports it.

items.prompt_en: Why does the writer imagine having sight for only a few days, and not for a whole life?
items.prompt_hi: Writer sirf kuch dino ki kalpana kyun karti hai, poori zindagi ki kyun nahi?
items.answer: A short time makes every sight feel precious, so readers realise how much they waste the sight they have
acceptable: so we value what we see
a short time makes us choose carefully
to make us realise how lucky we are
hints: What do you do when you have very little time?
Think of choosing what matters most.
Short time makes each sight more ___.
Few days make every sight precious, so we learn to value ours.

items.prompt_en: Explain to a younger child what Helen Keller wanted us to learn from 'Three Days to See'. Use one example from your own day.
items.prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko samjhao — Helen Keller hume kya sikhana chahti thi? Apne din ka ek example do.
items.answer: Helen Keller, who could not see or hear, reminds us to use and value our senses fully every day instead of taking them for granted
acceptable: do not take our senses for granted
use our senses fully every day
hints: Who was Helen Keller?
What do we forget to notice every day?
She wants us to ___ our senses.
She wants us to value our senses and not take them for granted.

items.prompt_en: Complete with the right verb forms: 'If I ___ (have) wings, I ___ (fly) over the mountains.'
items.prompt_hi: Ye kalpana hai. Khaali jagah bharo: 'If I ___ (have) wings, I ___ (fly)...'
items.answer: If I had wings, I would fly over the mountains.
acceptable: If I had wings, I would fly over the mountains
hints: Is this real or imagined?
Imagined: the if-part goes into the past.
If I ___ wings, I would ___.
If I had wings, I would fly over the mountains.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake: 'If I have three days to see, I would visit a museum.'
items.prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: 'If I have three days to see, I would visit a museum.'
items.answer: If I had three days to see, I would visit a museum.
acceptable: If I had three days to see, I would visit a museum.
hints: Is this real or imagined?
Look at the verb after 'If'.
If I ___ three days to see...
'Have' should be 'had': If I had three days to see, I would visit a museum.

items.prompt_en: Imagine you could not hear for a week. Make one sentence starting with 'If I could not hear...' using 'would'.
items.prompt_hi: Socho ek hafte tak sun nahi sakte. 'If I could not hear...' se ek line banao, 'would' ke saath.
items.answer: If I could not hear, I would miss the sound of my mother's voice.
acceptable: If I could not hear, I would miss music.
If I could not hear, I would use signs to talk.
If I could not hear, I would read lips.
If I couldn't hear, I would miss my friends' voices.
hints: What sound would you miss most?
Use 'would' + an action.
If I could not hear, I would ___.
For example: If I could not hear, I would miss my mother's voice.

items.prompt_en: Choose the right verb: 'I ___ (saw / watched) the sun slowly set behind the hills for half an hour.'
items.prompt_hi: Aadhe ghante tak dhyaan se dekha — 'saw' ya 'watched'?
items.answer: watched

The sun was moving slowly.
For something that moves and changes, we ___.
'Watched', because you kept looking at it as it changed.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake: 'Look the stars! They are shining.'
items.prompt_hi: Is line mein ek chhota word gaayab hai. Kaunsa? 'Look the stars!'
items.answer: Look at the stars! They are shining.
hints: Read it slowly. Does it sound complete?
'Look' needs a small word before what you look at.
Look ___ the stars!
Look at the stars: 'look' needs 'at'.

items.prompt_en: Say in English: 'Main dhyaan se pakshiyon ki awaaz sun rahi thi.' Use 'listen'.
items.prompt_hi: English mein bolo, 'listen' use karke: 'Main dhyaan se pakshiyon ki awaaz sun rahi thi.'
items.answer: I was listening carefully to the sounds of the birds.
acceptable: I was listening carefully to the birds.
I was carefully listening to the birds' sounds.
I was listening carefully to the birdsong.
I was listening to the birds carefully.
hints: Which tense: was -ing.
'Listen' needs a small word after it.
I was listening carefully ___ the birds.
I was listening carefully to the sounds of the birds.

items.prompt_en: After reading 'Three Days to See', a boy goes home. What might he do differently that evening?
items.prompt_hi: Ye lesson padhne ke baad ek ladka ghar gaya. Us shaam woh kya alag karega?
items.answer: He might notice things he usually ignores, like the colours of the sky or his family's faces, and value his senses
acceptable: he will look at his family's faces
he will pay attention to small things
hints: What did the writer wish she could see?
What do we usually ignore?
He might stop and ___ things around him.
He might notice everyday sights and value his senses more.

workedExample.problem: Turn this into an imagined (second conditional) sentence: 'I have one day to see. I visit the sea.'
steps: Decide: this is imagined, not real, so use the dream pattern.
If-part goes into the simple past: 'If I had one day to see'.
Result part uses would + base verb: 'I would visit the sea'.
Answer: If I had one day to see, I would visit the sea.
fadedVersion: Decide: this is ___, not real.
If-part goes into the simple past: 'If I ___ one day to see'.
Result part uses ___ + base verb.
Answer: If I ___ one day to see, I ___ the sea.

Name animal sounds and body signals in English (bark, neigh, moo, hoot, roar, chirp, wag)

expectations: Says the doctor learns to understand animals with help from his parrot
Explains that animals communicate through sounds and body movements, not words
Infers why animals trust the doctor (he understands them, so he can find what is wrong)
Uses at least one collective noun and one animal-sound verb correctly
Reports what a character said using 'said' or 'told' correctly

signs: Says 'She told that she was ill'
Says 'The parrot told, dogs can talk'
Never puts a person after 'told'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'The parrot told the doctor that dogs talk with their tails' or 'The parrot told that dogs talk with their tails'?

options.text: The parrot told the doctor that dogs talk with their tails.
The parrot told that dogs talk with their tails.

remediation.representation: An arrow card: 'told' always points at a person (told WHOM?); 'said' points at the words (said WHAT?)
remediation.moveShape: Child asks 'told whom?' after every 'told' sentence and fills the person; then sorts five sentences into said-boxes and told-boxes

misconceptions.belief: 'Said' can take a person directly, like Hindi 'mujhe kaha' ('He said me')
signs: Says 'She said me to come'
Says 'The doctor said us that...'
Drops 'to' after 'said'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'Mitthu said to me, Animals talk too' or 'Mitthu said me, Animals talk too'?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Hindi mein 'mujhse kaha' bolte hain. English mein 'said me' chalega ya 'said to me'?

options.text: Mitthu said to me, 'Animals talk too.'
Mitthu said me, 'Animals talk too.'

remediation.representation: A bridge picture: 'said' needs the little bridge 'to' to reach a person; 'told' reaches the person directly
remediation.moveShape: Child reads 'said __ me' and places the 'to' bridge; then swaps to 'told me' and sees no bridge is needed

misconceptions.belief: Any group word goes with any animal ('a herd of birds', 'a flock of bees')
signs: Says 'a herd of birds'
Says 'a group of fishes' for every case
Says 'a flock of cows'

diagnostic.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'a flock of birds' or 'a herd of birds'?
diagnostic.prompt_hi: Pakshiyon ke jhund ko English mein kya kehte hain — 'a flock of birds' ya 'a herd of birds'?

options.text: a flock of birds
a herd of birds

remediation.representation: Picture-word match board: each group picture (birds in the sky, cows in a field, bees round a hive) paired with its group word
remediation.moveShape: Child matches pictures to group words, then says each pair in a sentence; teacher mixes in one wrong pair for the child to catch

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Doctor Ramu liked animals more than people. One day his parrot Mitthu said, "Animals talk too. A dog talks with its tail, a cow with its ears." Soon the doctor understood them all, and sick animals came from far away to his clinic.' Who helped Doctor Ramu understand the animals?
items.prompt_hi: Kahani suno. Doctor Ramu ko jaanwaron ki baat samajhne mein kisne madad ki?
items.answer: His parrot Mitthu
hints: Which animal speaks in the story?
It is a bird that can copy words.
His ___ Mitthu helped him.
His parrot Mitthu helped him.

items.prompt_en: Read: 'Doctor Ramu liked animals more than people. One day his parrot Mitthu said, "Animals talk too. A dog talks with its tail, a cow with its ears." Soon the doctor understood them all, and sick animals came from far away to his clinic.' Why did sick animals come from far away to his clinic?
items.prompt_hi: Door-door se beemaar jaanwar unke clinic kyun aate the?
items.answer: Because he could understand them, so he could find out what was wrong and treat them
acceptable: he knew what was wrong with them
hints: What special skill did the doctor learn?
Think about why a patient likes a doctor who listens.
He could ___ what the animals said.
He understood them, so he could find what was wrong.

items.prompt_en: A cow comes to the clinic holding one ear down and swishing her tail slowly. Using the parrot's idea, what will the doctor do first?
items.prompt_hi: Ek gaay aayi, ek kaan neeche, poonch dheere hilaati. Doctor pehle kya karega?
items.answer: He will watch her ears and tail to understand how she feels and what hurts
acceptable: he will look at her ears
he will read her body signals
he will try to understand her
hints: What did the parrot say a cow talks with?
So what should the doctor look at?
He will watch her ___.
He will read her ears and tail to understand what is wrong.

items.prompt_en: Fill in the blank: 'A ___ of birds flew over the clinic.'
items.prompt_hi: Khaali jagah: 'A ___ of birds flew over the clinic.' Pakshiyon ka jhund?
items.answer: flock
hints: What do we call a group of birds?
It rhymes with 'clock'.
A fl___ of birds.
A flock of birds.

items.prompt_en: Which is correct: 'a herd of cows' or 'a flock of cows'?
items.prompt_hi: Gaayon ka jhund — 'herd' ya 'flock'?
items.answer: a herd of cows
hints: Is 'flock' for animals on the ground or birds?
Cows and elephants have their own word.
A h___ of cows.
A herd of cows; flock is for birds and sheep.

items.prompt_en: Fill in the blank: 'A ___ of bees buzzed around the hive.'
items.prompt_hi: Madhumakkhiyon ke jhund ke liye kaunsa word?
items.answer: swarm
hints: Think of a buzzing, moving cloud.
It starts with 'sw'.
A sw___ of bees.
A swarm of bees.

items.prompt_en: Fill in 'said' or 'told': 'The parrot ___ the doctor a secret.'
items.prompt_hi: 'said' ya 'told'? 'The parrot ___ the doctor a secret.' Dhyaan do — kisko bataya?
items.answer: told
hints: Is there a person right after the blank?
Which word can take a person directly?
The parrot ___ the doctor (told whom?).
'Told', because a person comes right after it.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake: 'The parrot said me that dogs talk with their tails.'
items.prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: 'The parrot said me that...'
items.answer: The parrot told me that dogs talk with their tails.
acceptable: The parrot told me that dogs talk with their tails.
The parrot said to me that dogs talk with their tails.
hints: Look at the words right after 'said'.
'Said' cannot take 'me' directly.
The parrot ___ me / said ___ me.
Say 'told me' or 'said to me'.

items.prompt_en: Which is correct, and why: 'She told that she was ill' or 'She said that she was ill'?
items.prompt_hi: Kaunsa sahi hai, aur kyun?
items.answer: 'She said that she was ill', because 'told' needs a person after it
acceptable: She said that she was ill.
said, because told needs a person
hints: Does 'told' have a person after it here?
Ask: told whom?
'Told' needs a ___ after it.
'She said that she was ill': told must be followed by a person.

items.prompt_en: In Hindi we say 'kutta bhaunkta hai'. In English, what does a dog do?
items.prompt_hi: Hindi mein 'kutta bhaunkta hai'. English mein kya kahenge?
items.answer: A dog barks.
hints: Say the dog's sound.
Woof woof is called...
A dog b___.
A dog barks.

items.prompt_en: Match each animal to its sound word: horse, owl, lion. Choose from: hoots, roars, neighs.
items.prompt_hi: Jaanwar aur awaaz milaao: horse, owl, lion — hoots, roars, neighs.
items.answer: A horse neighs, an owl hoots, a lion roars.
acceptable: horse neighs, owl hoots, lion roars
hints: Start with the one you are sure of.
The owl's sound comes at night: hoo-hoo.
Horse ___, owl ___, lion ___.
Horse neighs, owl hoots, lion roars.

items.prompt_en: Explain to your younger cousin what the story of the animal doctor teaches us about how animals communicate. Give one example.

items.answer: Animals communicate with sounds and body movements, like a dog wagging its tail; if we watch and listen carefully, we can understand them
acceptable: a dog wags its tail when happy
we must watch animals carefully to understand them
hints: How does your pet or a street dog show it is happy?
Think of tails, ears and sounds.
Animals talk with their ___ and sounds.
They communicate through sounds and body signals we can learn to read.

workedExample.problem: Report this using 'told': Mitthu said to the doctor, 'Animals talk too.'
steps: Find who is speaking (Mitthu) and who is listening (the doctor).

'Told' must be followed directly by the ___.
Add '___' and the message.

Because the man had a real problem with his feet
Because the poet made a mistake

a banana is not a spoon
it is the opposite of normal

Can a banana do that job?

It is impossible and surprising, and surprise makes us laugh.

items.answer: ABAB

Does line 1 rhyme with line 2 or line 3?
Ludhiana-banana = A, ears-years = ___

items.prompt_hi: 'ears' ke saath kaunsa rhyme karta hai — 'years' ya 'eyes'?
items.answer: years

ears, y-___

acceptable: wear his blanket as a hat
use a pan as a pillow
hints: What does a normal person do at bedtime?

items.prompt_en: Choose the right word: 'He laughed ___ (loud / loudly) at his own joke.'
items.prompt_hi: 'loud' ya 'loudly'? Kaise hasa — yeh batane wala word?
items.answer: loudly
acceptable: He laughed loudly at his own joke.

'Loudly', because it tells how he laughed.

items.prompt_en: Find the mistake: 'The funny man danced very good at the wedding.'
items.prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: 'danced very good'.

acceptable: The funny man danced very well at the wedding.

'Good' describes things; actions need another word.
He danced very ___.

items.prompt_en: Compare: 'He is a slow walker' and 'He walks slowly.' In each sentence, what does the describing word describe?
items.prompt_hi: Dono sentences mein 'slow' aur 'slowly' kisko describe kar rahe hain?
items.answer: 'Slow' describes the noun 'walker'; 'slowly' describes the verb 'walks'
acceptable: slow describes walker, slowly describes walks
slow is an adjective, slowly is an adverb
hints: Find the naming word in sentence one.
Find the action word in sentence two.
Slow tells about the ___, slowly tells about the ___.
Slow describes the walker; slowly describes how he walks.

items.prompt_en: The funny man does everything 'ulta'. Give the English opposites of: up, wet, front.

items.answer: down, dry, back

Think of clothes after the sun dries them.
up-___, wet-___, front-___
Down, dry, back.

items.prompt_en: Why do nonsense poets so often use opposites and exaggeration, like crying 'for years'?
items.prompt_hi: Nonsense kavi ulti baatein aur 'for years' jaisi badha-chadha ke baatein kyun karte hain?
items.answer: Because breaking what we expect surprises us, and surprise and exaggeration make us laugh
hints: Can anyone really cry for years?
What do we feel when something unexpected happens?
Opposites and exaggeration create ___.
They break our expectations, and that surprise makes us laugh.

items.prompt_en: What does 'rhyme scheme' mean?

pattern of rhyming words at the end of lines

it makes us laugh with impossible things
it uses funny impossible actions with rhyme
hints: What strange thing did the Ludhiana man do?
Is it meant to be real?
A nonsense poem is silly on ___.
It is silly on purpose, with rhyme and rhythm, so the surprise makes us laugh.
